id: To J.G. On the News of His Marriage

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My Love? alas! I must not call you Mine, But to your envy’d Bride that Name resign: I must forget your lovely melting Charms, And be for ever Banisht from your Arms: For ever? oh! the Horror of that Sound! It gives my bleeding Heart a deadly wound: While I might hope, although my Hope was vain, It gave some Ease to my unpitty’d Pain, But now your Hymen doth all Hope exclude, And but to think is Sin; yet you intrude On every Thought; if I but close my Eyes, Methinks your pleasing Form besides me lies; With every Sigh I gently breath your Name, Yet no ill Thoughts pollute my hallow’d Flame; ’Tis pure and harmless, as a Lambent Fire, And never mingled with a warm Desire: All I have now to ask of Bounteous Heaven, Is, that your Perjuries may be forgiven: That she who you have with your Nuptials blest, As She’s the Happiest Wife, may prove the Best: That all our Joys may light on you alone, Then I can be contented to have none: And never wish that you shou’d kinder be, Than now and then, to cast a Thought on Me: And, Madam, though the Conquest you have won, Over my Strephon, has my hopes undone; I’le daily beg of Heaven, he may be Kinder to You, than he has been to Me.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Love, Mine, But

outputs.L1:
My love—alas, I must no longer call you mine,  
But must resign that name to your envied bride.  
I must forget your lovely, melting charms,  
And be forever banished from your arms.  

Forever—oh, the horror of that word!  
It strikes a mortal wound within my bleeding heart.  
While I could hope, though all my hope was vain,  
It brought some ease to my unpitied pain;  
But now your Hymen excludes all hope,  
And even thought itself becomes a sin.  

Yet still you intrude upon my every thought.  
If I but close my eyes, it seems  
Your pleasing form lies beside me.  
With every sigh, I softly breathe your name;  
Yet no unworthy thought pollutes my hallowed flame.  
It is pure and harmless, like a lambent fire,  
And never mingled with a warmer desire.  

All I have now to ask of bounteous Heaven  
Is that your perjuries may be forgiven;  
That she whom you have blessed with your nuptials,  
As she is the happiest wife, may prove the best;  
That all our joys may rest on you alone—  
Then I can be content to have none.  

I shall never wish that you be kinder to me  
Than, now and then, to cast a thought my way.  
And, Madam, though the conquest you have won  
Over my Strephon has undone my hopes,  
I shall daily beg of Heaven  
That he may be kinder to you  
Than he has been to me.
outputs.L2:
My beloved—no, sadly, I no longer have the right to call you mine. I must surrender that title to the bride whom others may well envy. I must force myself to forget your tender, enchanting charms and accept that I am banished from your embrace forever.

Forever—how dreadful that word sounds. It strikes a mortal blow to my wounded heart. While I could still hope, even though that hope was empty, it gave a little comfort to my unpitied suffering. But now your marriage has shut out every possibility of hope, and even thinking of you feels like a sin. Still, you enter every thought I have. If I merely close my eyes, I seem to see your dear figure lying beside me. With every sigh, I softly breathe your name.

Yet no guilty thought stains the sacred love I bear you. It is innocent and pure, like a harmless flickering flame, never joined with passionate desire. All I can now ask from generous Heaven is that your broken vows may be pardoned; that the woman you have blessed with marriage, being the happiest of wives, may also prove the best; and that every joy meant for us may fall upon you alone. If that happens, I can be satisfied to have none myself.

I will not even wish for more kindness from you than this: that now and then you might spare a thought for me. And, madam, though your victory in winning my Strephon has destroyed all my hopes, I will pray each day to Heaven that he may be kinder to you than he has been to me.
outputs.L3:
The speaker mourns the painful truth that she can no longer claim her beloved as her own. Once, she may have felt that his heart belonged to her, but now he belongs to another: his bride. This realization fills her with sorrow, not only because she has lost him, but because the loss is final. She is forever shut out from his embrace, banished from the comfort of his love, and forced to give up every hope she once cherished.

Even so, she cannot keep her thoughts from returning to him. His memory remains constant in her heart, and her affection has not disappeared simply because he has chosen someone else. Yet she insists that her love is not impure or sinful. Though she still loves him deeply, her feeling is spiritual rather than selfish; it is free from wrongful desire and does not seek to disturb his marriage.

In her grief, she turns to prayer. She asks that his betrayals and wrongdoings may be forgiven, showing that her love is generous even after she has been hurt. She also prays for his wife, hoping that the bride will be happy and worthy of him. Rather than cursing the woman who now has the place she once longed for, the speaker tries to bless her and wish her peace.

Most movingly, the speaker’s heartbreak does not turn into bitterness. Though she has suffered because of him, she still wishes him joy. She hopes that he will be happy in his new life and that he will treat his wife with more kindness and faithfulness than he showed to her. Her words reveal a sorrowful but noble love: one that grieves deeply, yet still chooses forgiveness, blessing, and selfless hope over resentment.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the voice of a rejected lover mourning the loss of Strephon, who has given himself to another in marriage. Speaking in a direct and intensely emotional address, the speaker confronts the pain of seeing the beloved united with his bride while she is left alone with her grief. Her words are shaped by the tension between desire and restraint: she still loves Strephon deeply, but his marriage has made that love forbidden. What was once hope has become renunciation, and the speaker must struggle to silence her longing in the name of virtue, purity, and moral duty.

Throughout the lament, the speaker’s sorrow is not expressed as anger alone, but as a mixture of heartbreak, tenderness, and wounded dignity. Strephon’s choice feels like a betrayal, yet she refuses to let her suffering become destructive. Instead of cursing the marriage or wishing misery upon the couple, she turns her grief into a prayer. She asks that Strephon and his bride may be happy, even though their happiness depends upon her own loss. This act of blessing reveals the depth of her love: it is no longer possessive, but self-sacrificing.

By the end, the speaker’s emotional struggle becomes a moral victory. She acknowledges the pain of abandonment, but she also accepts the boundaries imposed by marriage and conscience. Her love survives, but it is transformed into forgiveness and resignation. The poem therefore portrays heartbreak not merely as personal suffering, but as a test of character. In choosing to pray for the happiness of the one who has wounded her, the speaker turns betrayed affection into an expression of spiritual discipline, generosity, and moral restraint.
outputs.L5:
Love is a word that can feel both simple and endless. It can be soft, like a quiet morning, or strong enough to change the direction of a life. When someone says, “You are mine,” it can sound like devotion, a promise to stay close and protect what matters.

But love should never be a cage. It should not take away freedom, dreams, or the right to be yourself. True love says, “You are mine” not as possession, but as belonging—two hearts choosing each other every day.

Love is mine when I give it freely. Love is yours when you receive it honestly. But the most beautiful love is the one we share, without fear, without force, and without losing who we are.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an 18th-century-style heroic couplet poem in the voice of a heartbroken woman addressing her former lover, who has married another, full of archaic spelling and diction.
counterfactuals.output:
False Strephon, now thy perjur’d Vows are fled,  
And Hymen crowns another’s happier Bed;  
Go, lead thy Bride where gaudy Tapers shine,  
Nor think what Tears disgrace these Eyes of mine.  

Ah! once thy Tongue, with soft delusive Art,  
Pour’d golden Treason round my yielding Heart;  
Thou call’dst me Fairest, swor’st by Stars above,  
No Time should waste, no Fortune conquer Love.  

Now those dear Oaths, like Morning Vapours, die,  
And all my promis’d Heav’n forsakes the Sky;  
Another wears the Smile for me design’d,  
Another triumphs o’er thy alter’d Mind.  

What tho’ her Cheeks with fresher Roses glow,  
Can blooming Youth more faithful Passion show?  
What tho’ her Dower thy sordid Friends approve,  
Can Lands repay the bankrupt Soul of Love?  

Take then thy Wealth, thy vain domestic Peace,  
Thy gilded Chains, and bid Remembrance cease;  
Yet when at Ev’n her Hand in thine is laid,  
Think on the Maid thy perfidy betray’d.  

Think, when her Musick courts thy careless Ear,  
Mine was the Voice thou once didst call sincere;  
Think, when she smiles, how oft my Smiles were thine,  
And blush to find thy Bliss was built on mine.  

For me, no more shall sprightly Hours advance,  
No more my Foot shall tempt the circling Dance;  
Pale Melancholy claims her silent Part,  
And folds her sable Mantle round my Heart.  

Yet go, ungrateful! since the Fates decree  
Thy guilty Joys, and spotless Woes for me;  
I ask not Vengeance from th’ offended Skies—  
Too soon thy Conscience shall become mine Eyes.  

Then shall my Image haunt thy midnight Rest,  
A mournful Visitant, an injur’d Guest;  
And she, who won thee from a Heart so true,  
May learn how little Faith is found in you.  

Farewel—tho’ still that Word my Soul doth rend,  
Farewel, my once ador’d, my faithless Friend;  
May Heav’n forgive what I can ne’er forget,  
And bless the Hand that leaves me to Regret.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dramatic monologue like an Augustan-era love elegy where a rejected speaker renounces her beloved after his wedding but still prays for his happiness.
counterfactuals.output:
Beloved once—no, let that title die,  
And with the myrtle at thy threshold lie.  
This day the torches flame, the viols sound,  
And Hymen scatters roses on the ground;  
While I, far off, with unregarded pain,  
Count every triumph of the happy train.  

Go, perjured heart—yet be not wretched: go;  
I loose the chain that bound me to my woe.  
No more my trembling hand shall seek thy name,  
No more my cheek confess its foolish flame;  
The vows I treasured, like the leaves of spring,  
I give to winds that know not where they wing.  

She takes the hand I dreamed one day was mine;  
Her brow receives the wreath I helped entwine.  
Smile on her, Heaven; let no remembered sigh  
Steal from my wrongs to cloud her bridal eye.  
If she can bless thee with a calmer breast,  
Be thou, in loving and in being loved, blest.  

Yet, O ye gods, who hear the forsaken pray,  
Turn not in wrath from his auspicious day.  
Let no pale Discord haunt his quiet board,  
No cold suspicion whisper at his word;  
Let fruitful seasons crown his chosen fields,  
And peace attend whatever fortune yields.  

As for this heart—too proud at last to plead—  
I tear thy image out, though I may bleed.  
My tears shall wash the altar where they fell,  
My silence be the last and stern farewell.  
Live, then; be glad; be constant, if thou can:  
I lose a lover, but forgive the man.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Restoration/early Georgian poem about unrequited love, betrayal, and resignation, using names like Strephon and formal rhyming couplets.
counterfactuals.output:
**Strephon Forsaken**

When Strephon first to Celia’s lattice came,  
He fed his sighs upon a hopeless flame;  
With vows well-turn’d, and tears discreetly shed,  
He crown’d the tyrant idol of his head.  

She heard him plead, and smiling seem’d to yield,  
Then bore his heart triumphant from the field;  
Her eyes gave promise, though her tongue denied,  
And half her scorn was art, and half was pride.  

But Damon came, with equipage and gold,  
And all those charms that make the wanton bold;  
At once her faith, like April blossoms, flew,  
False to the hand by which it fairer grew.  

Poor Strephon saw, yet would not credit pain,  
And call’d her perjury a lover’s stain;  
Till at the ball, beneath the blazing light,  
She gave to Damon what was his by right—  

That glance, that fan, that whisper’s soft command,  
The yielding pressure of her faithless hand.  
Then from his breast the fond illusion fell,  
And love, long blind, grew sensible of hell.  

“Go, perjur’d fair,” he cried, “pursue thy prize;  
Let richer incense court thy practis’d eyes.  
I blame not thee: the world and thou agree;  
Gold buys the heart that virtue leaves too free.  

“No more my verse shall teach thy name to live,  
Nor beg that pity thou couldst never give.  
Since truth is poor, and constancy a jest,  
I’ll seek that calm which dwells in no fond breast.  

“Yet should some hour, when flatterers are gone,  
When Damon sleeps, and thou art left alone,  
One tender thought of Strephon cross thy mind,  
Be just at last, and own I was too kind.”  

He spoke; then bow’d with ceremonious air,  
And hid his anguish in a mien severe.  
So exil’d courtiers, ruin’d yet polite,  
Smile on the world, and perish out of sight.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imitate the style of a sentimental 1700s female poet: the narrator must tell her lost love she cannot call him hers anymore, bless his bride, and ask only to be remembered sometimes.
counterfactuals.output:
My once dear Lord—no more my own,  
That tender name I must resign;  
The vows I whisper’d, all are flown,  
And other hopes are fix’d with thine.

Yet, though my heart in silence bleed,  
No murmuring curse shall stain my tongue;  
May Heaven her gentle footsteps lead,  
For whom thy bridal wreath is hung.

May she be fair in every grace  
That makes the wedded bosom blest;  
May peace sit smiling on her face,  
And love lie constant in her breast.

I ask not now thy sighs, thy tears,  
Nor one fond look to bid me live;  
I only ask, in after years,  
One little thought thou yet may’st give.

When evening shades thy window close,  
When music wakes some plaintive strain,  
Think—there was one, who hid her woes,  
And bless’d thee, though she lov’d in vain.

Then let my name, by chance exprest,  
Not wound thy joy, nor cloud thy brow;  
But pass, like perfume from the breast  
Of some pale flower forgotten now.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an archaic English poem in rhymed couplets from a woman to the man who abandoned her for marriage, expressing sorrow without lust and ending with a blessing for his new wife.
counterfactuals.output:
Thou went’st where bridal torches softly burn,  
And left me with the dusk and no return.  

I blame thee not, though tears my vigil keep;  
The heart may break, yet teach the tongue to sleep.  

No wanton fire within my bosom lies,  
But chastened grief that lifteth patient eyes.  

I loved thee once with honour’s quiet breath,  
And mourn thee now as one might mourn a death.  

The vows we dreamed are scattered like the rain,  
Yet I will bear their memory without stain.  

Go thou in peace; let no old shadow start  
To trouble her who holdeth now thy heart.  

May Heaven make her days with gladness rife,  
And bless, for thee, thy chosen wedded wife.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
